author: Marcus R. Brown
description:
`JobControlSystem` started a 30-second cleanup interval in its constructor and discarded the handle:

```ts
private startCleanupTimer(): void {
  setInterval(() => {
    this.cleanup()
  }, 30000) // Run cleanup every 30 seconds
}
```

No `clearInterval` anywhere, and `JobController` had no disposal method — so the timer ran until its execution context died.

## Blast radius

Bounded in production. `ShellEnvironment`'s constructor creates the controller, `shell.worker.ts` creates one environment, and `App.tsx:97` calls `worker.terminate()`, which tears the interval down with the worker.

The real accumulation is in tests. `job-controller.test.ts` builds a controller per test, and every suite that constructs a `ShellEnvironment` builds another — each leaking an interval into the vitest process for the length of the run.

Proven rather than asserted: spying on `cleanup()` and advancing fake timers by 5 × 30s against an undisposed controller records exactly 5 invocations. After `dispose()`, the same advance records 0.

## Change

Stores the handle as `ReturnType<typeof setInterval>`, which covers both the DOM and Node timer types — relevant here because this runs inside a Web Worker.

Adds `dispose()` to `JobController` and implements it idempotently, clearing the stored handle so a second call is a no-op. `ShellEnvironment` owns the controller, so it gains a matching `dispose()` that delegates — naming follows `Terminal.tsx`, which already uses `dispose()`.

Tests now dispose in `afterEach`.

## Deliberately not done

**No worker teardown was added.** `shell.worker.ts` has no `close` handler, `self.onclose`, or shutdown message path. Inventing a worker lifecycle to call disposal would be scope creep for a leak that `terminate()` already handles — so production is untouched and the disposal contract exists for the owners that actually need it.
